text: What does phonetics study?
choices: The physical production and perception of speech sounds
The history of writing systems only
The social meanings of surnames
The grammar of written prose

text: What does phonology primarily study?
choices: How speakers breathe during exercise
How a language organizes speech sounds
The origins of alphabetic scripts
The meanings of individual names

text: Which organs normally provide the airstream for ordinary speech?
choices: The kidneys
The stomach
The lungs
The sinuses

text: Where are the vocal folds located?
choices: Behind the lips
In the nasal cavity
At the alveolar ridge
In the larynx

text: Which articulator is most directly involved in many tongue sounds?
choices: The tongue
The eardrum
The kneecap
The soft palate only

text: What place of articulation uses both lips?
choices: Dental
Bilabial
Velar
Glottal

text: What is the alveolar ridge?
choices: The opening between the vocal folds
The back wall of the throat
The ridge just behind the upper teeth
The center of the hard palate

text: What does the velum help control?
choices: Whether the lips round
Whether the vocal folds vibrate
Whether a syllable receives stress
Whether air can pass through the nose

text: What is the glottis?

The tip of the tongue
The passage between the teeth
The lower lip muscle

text: What generally distinguishes a consonant from a vowel in articulation?
choices: A consonant must always be voiced
A consonant involves greater constriction of the airstream
A vowel must always be written with a single letter
A vowel is made only with the lips

text: What happens to the vocal folds during a voiced sound?
choices: They close the nasal passage permanently
They touch the teeth
They vibrate

text: What is the International Phonetic Alphabet designed to represent?
choices: Only the spelling of English
The world's writing systems by age
The meanings of grammatical morphemes
Speech sounds with standardized symbols

Voiced bilabial nasal

choices: Voiceless dental fricative
Voiced bilabial stop
Voiced velar nasal
Voiceless alveolar lateral

text: How is the IPA symbol /m/ commonly classified?
choices: Alveolar trill
Velar stop
Bilabial nasal
Labiodental fricative

text: How is the IPA symbol /k/ commonly classified?
choices: Voiced bilabial stop
Voiceless postalveolar fricative
Voiced dental nasal
Voiceless velar stop

text: How is the IPA symbol /f/ commonly classified?
choices: Voiceless labiodental fricative
Voiced bilabial stop
Voiceless velar nasal
Voiced alveolar trill

text: What sound is conventionally represented by IPA /ʃ/?
choices: A voiced bilabial nasal
A voiceless postalveolar fricative
A voiceless dental stop
A voiced velar stop

text: How is /ŋ/ commonly classified?
choices: Voiceless bilabial stop
Voiced dental fricative
Voiced velar nasal
Alveolar lateral approximant

text: What is a diphthong?
choices: A consonant with two closures
A syllable with two separate stresses
A pair of unrelated phonemes
A vowel involving movement between two qualities

text: What is the nucleus of a syllable?
choices: Its central sonorous element, often a vowel
Its initial consonant cluster
Its final consonant only
Its written accent mark

text: What is the onset of a syllable?
choices: The vowel's formant pattern
The consonant material before the nucleus
The final consonant material
The syllable's pitch movement

text: What is the coda of a syllable?
choices: The first vowel in a word
The syllable's onset cluster
The consonant material after the nucleus
The speaker's regional accent

text: What does lexical stress usually indicate?
choices: A mandatory pause between clauses
A change from consonant to vowel
The spelling origin of a word
A relatively prominent syllable within a word

text: What is intonation?
choices: The pattern of pitch across an utterance
The number of consonants in a syllable
The speed of lip movement only
The historical replacement of a sound

text: In linguistics, what is an accent?
choices: A mark that must appear over every stressed vowel
A patterned way of pronouncing a language associated with speakers or groups
A synonym for a writing system
A universal rule for correct pronunciation

text: What is a minimal pair?
choices: Two synonyms with different spellings
Two dialects with identical pronunciation
Two forms differing in one sound in the same position with different meanings
Two syllables that always receive stress

text: What is a phoneme?
choices: Any audible noise made by a speaker
A letter used in an alphabet
A syllable without a vowel
A contrastive sound category in a particular language

text: What is an allophone?
choices: A contextual or variable realization of a phoneme
A separate writing system
A word borrowed from another language
A unit larger than a sentence

text: What is assimilation in sound change or speech?
choices: A sound becomes less like every neighbor
One sound becomes more like a neighboring sound
A word changes its meaning through metaphor
A syllable gains a new written symbol

text: What is dissimilation?
choices: Two identical words merge into one
A vowel loses all pitch
A sound becomes less like another nearby sound
A consonant becomes a written digraph

text: What is epenthesis?
choices: Deletion of a final syllable
Reversal of two adjacent sounds
Replacement of a noun by a verb
Insertion of a sound into a word or sequence

text: What is sound deletion, or elision?
choices: Loss of a sound in a particular context
Insertion of an extra vowel
Movement of stress to the first syllable
A change from stop to fricative

text: What is metathesis?
choices: A change in which vowels become nasal
A change in which sounds exchange positions
A rule assigning grammatical gender
A shift from oral to written tradition

text: What are cognates?
choices: Words borrowed from the same modern publisher
Words that always rhyme
Words inherited from a common ancestral form
Different spellings of one current word

text: What is a regular sound change?
choices: A change that affects only one famous word
A spelling reform imposed by a school
A change that happens identically in every language
A sound correspondence that affects comparable environments systematically

text: What does Grimm's law describe?
choices: Major consonant correspondences between Proto-Indo-European and Germanic
The shift from Latin spelling to Greek spelling
A chain shift in modern American English vowels
The creation of the IPA

text: What is voicing assimilation?
choices: A vowel changes its height because of spelling
A sound becomes more like a neighboring sound in voicing
A consonant changes into a tone
A syllable gains an extra written letter

text: What is palatalization?
choices: A sound becomes pharyngeal
A syllable loses its nucleus
A sound moves toward a palatal or front-vowel-like articulation
A word changes from singular to plural

text: What is lenition?
choices: A strengthening process that always creates ejectives
The insertion of a tone-bearing vowel
A change limited to spelling
A weakening process such as stop-to-fricative change

text: What is lexical tone?
choices: Pitch differences that can distinguish word or morpheme meanings
Stress that always falls on the final syllable
A consonant contrast involving airflow
The melody of instrumental music

text: What is vowel harmony?
choices: A rule requiring every word to contain a diphthong
A pattern in which vowels within a word share selected features
The loss of vowels in unstressed syllables
A poetic rhyme between adjacent vowels

text: What does phonotactics describe?
choices: The historical family tree of languages
The meanings of phonetic symbols
The permitted combinations and positions of sounds in a language
The anatomy of the larynx

text: What is a language family?
choices: Languages spoken only by one biological family
Dialects with identical accents
Writing systems sharing the same alphabet
A group of languages descended from a common ancestor

text: What are distinctive features used for in phonological analysis?
choices: Representing sound contrasts with properties such as [voice] or [nasal]
Recording only a speaker's biography
Measuring word frequency in a corpus
Describing literary themes

text: What is a natural class of sounds?
choices: A group of sounds found only in nature
A group sharing a set of phonological features
A list of sounds ordered by spelling
A category based solely on word meaning

text: What does the sonority hierarchy generally rank?
choices: Words by historical age
Speakers by regional origin
Sounds by relative openness or resonance
Syllables by written length

text: What is a tone language?
choices: A language spoken only in singing
A language without consonants
A language whose words all have equal stress
A language in which pitch contrasts can distinguish lexical meaning

text: What is the usual purpose of an IPA transcription?
choices: To show pronunciation independently of ordinary spelling
To encode a sentence's syntax
To identify a speaker's ancestry
To replace all spoken language with writing

text: What is a speech community?
choices: A group that speaks only one possible accent
A group sharing norms about language use and interpretation
A biological population with identical vocal tracts
A community whose language has no variation

text: What is a distinctive feature such as [voice]?
choices: A punctuation mark in phonetic spelling
A measure of sentence length
An abstract property used to characterize and contrast sounds
A rule about politeness

text: What is feature spreading?
choices: The distribution of a new alphabet across countries
The loss of all features from unstressed speech
The movement of a word between dialects
The extension of a phonological feature from one segment to another

text: What does markedness refer to in phonological theory?
choices: The relative structural complexity or special status of a form
Whether a sound is written with a diacritic
How loudly a speaker produces a segment
Whether a word is legally registered

text: What is a syllabic consonant?
choices: A consonant written with two letters
A consonant functioning as the nucleus of a syllable
A consonant that can never be voiced
A consonant occurring only in a coda

text: What is a mora?
choices: A type of consonant closure
A word-initial accent mark
A unit of syllable weight used in descriptions of quantity and timing
A language family subgroup

text: What is a trochee in metrical phonology?
choices: A foot with two equally strong syllables
A syllable containing a long consonant
A sequence of three rising tones
A foot with a strong syllable followed by a weak one

text: What is a pitch-accent system?
choices: A system in which a restricted pitch contrast helps mark prominence
A system in which every syllable has identical pitch
A writing system using acute accents only
A stress system with no phonetic pitch differences

text: What is tone sandhi?
choices: A consonant mutation caused by spelling
A tone alternation triggered by neighboring tones or a prosodic context
The replacement of stress by vowel harmony
A historical merger of two alphabets

text: What is downstep in tone phonology?
choices: A loss of tone from every unstressed syllable
A downward movement of the tongue
A systematic lowering of the pitch level of a following tone
A spelling convention for falling intonation

text: What is vowel reduction?
choices: A process that lengthens every stressed vowel
A shift from oral to nasal consonants
The deletion of a word-final consonant
A decrease in vowel articulatory distinctness, often in weak positions

text: What is coarticulation?
choices: The overlap of articulatory gestures for neighboring sounds
The use of two writing systems in one text
The merger of two unrelated languages
The repetition of a syllable for emphasis

text: What does voice onset time measure?
choices: The duration of a whole utterance
The interval between a stop release and the onset of vocal-fold vibration
The pitch difference between two vowels
The distance between the lips and teeth

text: What do the first two formants, F1 and F2, help describe acoustically?
choices: Stop closure duration only
Word frequency
Vowel quality
Syllable count

text: What is a spectrogram?
choices: A diagram of a language family
A chart of spelling irregularities
A map of tongue muscles
A visual display of acoustic energy across time and frequency

text: What physical property is most closely related to fundamental frequency?
choices: The rate of vocal-fold vibration
The place of tongue constriction
The duration of a syllable coda
The width of the oral cavity

text: What is aspiration in phonetics?
choices: A complete closure of the nasal passage
A period of increased breathy airflow associated with some consonants
A pitch movement from high to low
A vowel's change in tongue height

text: What is prenasalization?
choices: A nasal vowel followed by a glottal stop only
A process deleting all nasals before vowels
A nasal portion occurring before an oral stop or other consonant
A type of written diacritic

text: What is a lateral approximant?
choices: A sound made with two complete lip closures
A nasal stop at the glottis
A vowel articulated only with the jaw
A sound made with airflow passing around one or both sides of the tongue

text: What is the sonority sequencing principle?
choices: Syllables tend to rise in sonority toward the nucleus and fall afterward
Every syllable must begin with a fricative
Stress must fall on the most open vowel
All consonants must have equal resonance

text: What is resyllabification?

A change in which segments are assigned to neighboring syllables across a boundary
A replacement of a phoneme by its spelling
A rule assigning lexical tone to a morpheme

text: What is phonological neutralization?

The replacement of speech by writing
The loss of a contrast in a particular environment
The merging of two languages' vocabularies

text: What is an archiphoneme in structuralist analysis?

A sound with four simultaneous places of articulation
A historical spelling symbol
A representation of the shared properties of neutralized phonemes

text: What is rule ordering?

The alphabetical ordering of IPA symbols
The ranking of speakers by pronunciation
The order in which dictionaries list meanings

text: What is an opaque sound change?
choices: A change that affects only written language
A change whose surface result obscures the environment or motivation of an earlier rule
A change audible only under water
A change that creates no alternations

text: What is the comparative method used to reconstruct?
choices: The correct spelling of a modern dialect
The acoustic shape of one speaker's vowels
Earlier forms by comparing regular correspondences among related languages
The social prestige of a language

text: What does an asterisk before a reconstructed form signify in historical linguistics?

The form is borrowed from Greek
The form appears only in poetry
The form is reconstructed rather than directly attested

text: What is internal reconstruction?

Comparing unrelated languages across continents
Reconstructing a script from archaeological ink
Recovering a speaker's private vocabulary

text: What is analogical leveling?
choices: A regular sound change that affects every language
The reduction of an irregular alternation by extending one pattern across forms
The equalization of pitch within a phrase
The borrowing of a complete writing system

text: What is grammaticalization?

A sound change affecting only nouns

text: What is semantic bleaching?

The deletion of a word's final consonant

text: What is a chain shift?

A sequence of borrowed words from one language
A shift from prose to verse

text: What is a push chain in chain-shift theory?

text: What does Verner's law explain in Germanic historical phonology?

text: What is umlaut in historical Germanic linguistics?

text: What is areal diffusion?

text: What does a wave model of language change emphasize?

text: What is the bleeding relation between two phonological rules?

text: Why are regular sound correspondences important in reconstruction?

text: What is the difference between an innovation and a retention in historical linguistics?

text: What is fortition?

text: What is a long consonant often called in phonological description?

text: What is the basic contrast between phonetic and phonemic transcription?
